title: The Sicilian Sveshnikov — A Master Class

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5
beats.say: The Sveshnikov — once dismissed as anti-positional, now a main weapon at every level. With e5 Black kicks the d4-knight and stakes a bold claim: I will accept a hole on d5 and a backward d-pawn, and in return I take the bishop pair, piece activity, and the thundering f5 break.
beats.sayShort: e5 — claim activity for the d5 hole.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6
beats.say: The knight leaps to b5, eyeing the d6 and c7 squares, and Black must spend a move on d6 to deny it. This is the price of e5 — a slightly loose d6-pawn — but the b5-knight has nowhere stable to land and will soon be chased to the rim.
beats.sayShort: d6 stops the knight hitting c7.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5
beats.say: Bg5 pins the f6-knight and leans on d5; Black calmly plays a6, chasing the b5-knight to the miserable a3-square, then b5 grabs queenside space and pens the offside knight in. With each move Black's pieces come alive.
beats.sayShort: a6 and b5 — chase the knight to a3.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6
beats.say: White plants the knight on the d5-hole — the position's defining feature. But Black is unfazed: after the bishops trade on f6, the dark-squared bishop sits on f6 raking toward White's queenside, and Black owns the bishop pair with a clear plan.
beats.sayShort: Nd5 lands; the f6-bishop eyes the dark squares.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 c3 O-O Nc2 Bg5
beats.say: White supports the centre with c3 and reroutes the knight to c2 to fight for the dark squares; Black castles and swings the bishop to g5, preparing the f5 break. The battle is set: White nurses the d5-outpost, Black strikes with f5 and unleashes the two bishops.
beats.sayShort: Bg5 and f5 — Black's bishops and break.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 c3 O-O Nc2 Bg5
beats.say: This is the Sveshnikov's bargain: hand White the d5-square, and in return take the bishop pair, the half-open c-file, and the thundering f5 break. For decades it was called unsound; today it is one of Black's most trusted answers to the king's-pawn, precisely because the activity outweighs the hole.
beats.sayShort: Activity and f5 outweigh the d5 hole.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6
beats.say: Instead of retreating, White grabs the knight with Bxf6. After gxf6 Black's kingside pawns are doubled and battered — but look closer: Black gains the bishop pair, the half-open g-file, and a massive pawn centre with e5 and f5 still to come.
beats.sayShort: gxf6 — doubled pawns, but bishops and centre.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5
beats.say: White rushes the knight to the d5-hole; Black answers with f5, the thematic break, blasting open the centre and the f-file for the rook. The ugly doubled f-pawn turns into a battering ram.
beats.sayShort: f5 — the doubled pawn becomes a battering ram.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bd3 Be6 Qh5 Bg7
beats.say: Both sides develop toward the fight — Bd3 and Qh5 eye Black's loosened king, but Be6 challenges the proud d5-knight and Bg7 rakes the long diagonal toward White's king. Black's two bishops and open lines bring dangerous attacking chances of his own.
beats.sayShort: Be6 hits d5; Bg7 rakes the long diagonal.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Bxf6 gxf6 Nd5 f5 Bd3 Be6 Qh5 Bg7
beats.say: The early exchange is a true test of understanding: Black's structure looks wrecked, but the bishop pair, the open g-file, and the e5 and f5 pawn duo generate ferocious activity. Modern theory trusts Black fully — the dynamic factors more than pay for the doubled pawns.
beats.sayShort: Dynamics pay for the doubled pawns.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 c4
beats.say: The Chelyabinsk approach: instead of the modest c3, White slams down c4 — the bind. The idea is to clamp the b5-pawn and the queenside light squares, freeze Black's expansion, and cement the powerful knight on d5.
beats.sayShort: c4 — the bind, clamping b5 and d5.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 c4 b4
beats.say: Black refuses to be squeezed: b4. The pawn jabs at the c3-square and gains queenside space, carving out a protected post on c5 for a piece. The bind is challenged the moment it appears.
beats.sayShort: b4 — jab the bind, grab c5.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Ndb5 d6 Bg5 a6 Na3 b5 Nd5 Be7 Bxf6 Bxf6 c4 b4 Nc2 O-O
beats.say: White reroutes the knight to c2 to target the b4-pawn; Black castles, completing development with the bishop pair and a ready a5 and Be6 to follow. Against the bind, Black's trumps are the two bishops and the eternal f5 break.
beats.sayShort: Castle — the two bishops fight the bind.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3
beats.say: Not wanting a theoretical battle, White simply retreats the knight to f3 — the Anti-Sveshnikov. It is solid but unambitious: Black keeps the big e5 centre, develops freely, and reaches equal chances without memorising any deep theory.
beats.sayShort: Nf3 retreat — Black equalises easily.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 h6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O
beats.say: Black plays the useful h6 to deny g5, then develops naturally with Be7 and castling. With the centre secure and no White knight on d5, this is a comfortable, classical Sicilian where Black has nothing at all to fear.
beats.sayShort: h6 and Be7 — comfortable development.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 e5 Nf3 h6 Bc4 Be7 O-O O-O Qe2 Bc5 Be3 Bxe3
beats.say: Black even seizes the initiative — Bc5 develops actively, and after Be3 the trade on e3 leaves White with no advantage whatsoever. The Anti-Sveshnikov has handed Black a free, equal game; White's caution earned nothing.
beats.sayShort: Bxe3 — trade off, fully equal.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5
beats.say: The Kalashnikov — Black plays e5 immediately, before developing the knight to f6. It is the Sveshnikov's bolder cousin: Black grabs the centre at once and dares White to try to exploit the d5-hole.
beats.sayShort: e5 at once — the bold Kalashnikov.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7
beats.say: White checks in with Nb5 and clamps down with c4 — a Maroczy-style bind, since Black has no quick b5 here. Black develops calmly with d6 and Be7, and the game becomes a patient maneuvering struggle around the d5-square.
beats.sayShort: c4 binds; Black develops patiently.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7 N1c3 a6 Na3 Be6
beats.say: The knights shuffle — a6 chases the b5-knight to the offside a3-square — and Be6 challenges the key d5-square head-on. Black's pieces find their squares while White's a3-knight sits stranded on the rim.
beats.sayShort: Be6 — challenge d5, a3-knight offside.

beats.moves: e4 c5 Nf3 Nc6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 e5 Nb5 d6 c4 Be7 N1c3 a6 Na3 Be6 Nc2 Nf6 Be2 Rc8
beats.say: White reroutes to c2; Black completes with Nf6 and Rc8 onto the half-open c-file. The verdict: the bind gives White a pull, but Black is solid and active, with the c-file, the d5-fight, and a later f5 or b5 break for full counterplay.
beats.sayShort: Rc8 — the c-file and the d5-fight.
